title: Everything about the new COROS VERTIX 4 and the COROS API | Terra
summary: COROS opened a self-service API route in 2026. This guide covers the access paths, rate limits, biomarker data, and the payloads you get through Terra.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- **COROS opened up its API in 2026.** An official MCP server launched in May, gained FIT files and health time series in June, and gained write access for workouts in September. It is built for AI assistants, not as a backend for multi-user products.
- **There are three ways to reach COROS data.** A personal AI connection, the self-service MCP route, and a Partner API by application.
- **The Partner API allows 1,000 calls per minute.** Workout history reaches back three months, at 30 days per request.
- **Through Terra, COROS arrives as three payloads.** Activity, Daily and Sleep, polled every 5 to 10 minutes and posted to your webhook in the same schema as every other provider.
- **Nothing streams from the COROS cloud.** Live heart rate is only available over Bluetooth broadcast from the watch.
- **The VERTIX 4 changes the sensor, not the API.** It carries COROS's latest heart rate sensor, and its data arrives through the same endpoints as every other COROS watch.


## Which COROS devices the API covers


Every COROS device syncs into one COROS account, and API access is granted per account. You do not integrate a VERTIX 4 separately from a PACE 3. Terra's[COROS integration](https://tryterra.co/integrations/coros) covers any device COROS currently supports.


Device family Type What it contributes


VERTIX 4, VERTIX 2S GPS watch Activities, daily summaries, sleep


PACE 4 Pro, PACE 4, PACE Pro, PACE 3 GPS watch Activities, daily summaries, sleep


APEX 4, APEX 2, APEX 2 Pro GPS watch Activities, daily summaries, sleep


NOMAD GPS watch Activities, daily summaries, sleep


DURA 2 Solar Bike computer Cycling activities


HR Monitor Armband Heart rate for a paired watch or app


POD 2, bike speed and cadence sensors Sensors Extra running and cycling metrics inside an activity


The endpoint does not change between devices. What changes is which fields come back populated. A bike computer sends rides and no sleep. A watch with the newer heart rate sensor fills the same heart rate object as an older watch, with different accuracy.


## How COROS data gets out: three access paths


COROS now offers three ways to reach user data, and two of them are recent additions. The company frames access as a standard, non-discriminatory process aligned with GDPR and the EU Data Act, per its API application page.


Connect COROS to AI Build on COROS MCP Partner API


Who it is for One person and their own AI assistant Developers building apps Established platforms with many users


Approval None None, self-service Application and review


Auth OAuth 2.0 OAuth 2.0 OAuth 2.0 with issued client ID and secret


Delivery On request Your app polls Webhook push, about 5 minutes after a workout


Writes Workouts and training plans Workouts and training plans Activities, workouts, plans, GPX routes up to 50 MB


Documentation Public on GitHub Public on GitHub Reference shared after approval


### What the MCP route is, and what it is not


COROS runs an official MCP server at` mcp.coros.com/mcp` . It exists so a person can connect their COROS account to an AI assistant. Developers can also authenticate users against it with OAuth 2.0 and no application.


It is not built to be the backend of a multi-user product. There are no webhooks, so your app has to poll every user. FIT files are capped at 50 per user per day, and the rate limit is not published. COROS itself points platforms that need multi-user access to the Partner API, which requires an application and review.


Both routes leave you maintaining a COROS-specific integration: its auth flow, its limits and its data format, next to every other wearable you support. That is the work Terra's[COROS integration](https://tryterra.co/integrations/coros) removes. Terra manages the COROS credentials, pushes new data to your webhook, and returns it in the same schema as every other provider. The payload section further down shows what arrives.


### What COROS changed in its API during 2026


The MCP server did not exist at the start of the year. COROS has shipped five updates to it since May, per its MCP update blog.


Date Change


September 21, 2026 Write access. Create and edit training plans and workouts for road running, trail running and cycling. Plans must run 4 to 16 weeks.


June 22, 2026 Lap and segment data per activity. FIT file retrieval, capped at 50 requests per day. Time series for stress, sleep HRV and health checks. Menstrual cycle data.


May 19, 2026 Regional URLs consolidated into one endpoint,` mcp.coros.com/mcp` .


May 9, 2026 Connection through an installable skill package,` coros-mcp` on npm.


May 5, 2026 Launch. Workout records, fitness metrics (VO2 max, running power, threshold pace, race prediction), training load, recovery, sleep, daily heart rate, HRV, stress, profile and devices.


Two patterns are worth noting. COROS moved from summaries to raw files in seven weeks. And it added write access four months after launch.


Deletes are still not possible through the API. A plan or workout created by an app has to be removed by the user in the COROS app.


### What data is available


The[MCP tool guide](https://github.com/coroslab/COROS-MCP/blob/main/docs/en/tools.md) is the most detailed public description of what COROS exposes.


Category What you can read


Activities Activity list, per-activity detail, laps, custom time segments, original FIT files


Sleep Sleep score, duration, stages, awake time, naps


Heart Daily average heart rate, resting heart rate, overnight HRV with COROS's assessment


Stress and recovery Daily stress, intraday stress series, current recovery level


Health check Heart rate, HRV, stress, respiration rate and SpO2 from the latest wellness check


Cycle tracking Menstrual status, phases and cycle ranges


Fitness VO2 max, running level, threshold pace, race predictions, training load


Profile Basic profile and linked devices


The Partner API lists four core reads on its public page:` getUserInfo` ,` getWorkoutRecords` ,` getDailyData` and` getWorkoutDetailFit` . COROS does not publish the fields inside` getDailyData` . Whether it matches the MCP's health coverage is something to ask COROS directly.


### Only native COROS activities come through


COROS delivers activities recorded on a COROS device. Manually uploaded and third-party activities are excluded, according to[Terra's COROS documentation](https://docs.tryterra.co/faq/help-topics/no-data/historical-backfill-returns-nothing/coros-limited-history-and-native-only) . If a user imports a ride from another platform into COROS, you will not see it.


## COROS API rate limits and historical data


The Partner API allows 1,000 calls per minute, and workout history reaches back three months. Those are the two numbers to design around.


Limit Build on COROS MCP Partner API


Rate limit Not published 1,000 calls per minute


Workout history Date-range queries, default last 7 days 3-month historical data


FIT files 50 per user per 24 hours, 10 maximum per call Available, no cap available


Overnight HRV, stress series, health check 7 days maximum per query Not published


Training plan detail 28 days per call Not published


List pagination 50 records per page Not published


### Three months is short


The` getWorkoutRecords` call covers at most 30 days per request and looks back three months. A full backfill for one user is therefore three or four calls. At 1,000 calls per minute the rate limit will rarely be the constraint. The lookback is.


For comparison,[Terra's documentation](https://docs.tryterra.co/help-center/help-topics/connecting/connection-errors-and-api-responses/webhook-30s-timeout-and-historical-data) lists Garmin at up to five years of history and Polar at 30 days. COROS sits between them, closer to Polar.


This matters for any product that needs a baseline. Training load models, HRV trends and injury risk scores all want more than 90 days. With COROS, you start with one quarter and build forward.


### The 24-hour rule


There is a second condition. Through Terra, COROS history is available up to three months back, or 24 hours before the user authenticated, whichever limit is hit first. The likely cause is a choice the user makes during sign-in.


COROS shows a historical data consent prompt in its OAuth flow. It does not return the user's choice in the token response. So you cannot tell from the connection alone whether history was granted.


The workaround from[Terra's docs](https://docs.tryterra.co/faq/help-topics/data-api-sdk/historical-data-and-backfill/coros-historical-consent-not-surfaced) is practical. After a user connects, request a small backfill for a date before the authentication date. If it comes back empty, the user likely declined historical access.


### What to do about it


- **Backfill on day one.** The window moves forward every day. Data you do not request now may be out of reach later.
- **Request in 30-day slices.** That matches the per-request maximum.
- **Store what you pull.** You cannot fetch it again once it ages past three months.
- **Test for consent.** Run the small backfill check after every new COROS connection.


## What COROS data looks like through Terra


Terra delivers COROS data as three normalized payload types: Activity, Daily and Sleep. The schema is the same one Terra uses for Garmin, Polar, Suunto and every other provider, so a COROS user needs no separate parser.


### How the data reaches you


1. The user connects COROS through the Terra widget. Terra manages the COROS API credentials, so there is nothing to register with COROS.
2. COROS does not notify Terra when data changes. Terra polls COROS every 5 to 10 minutes for each connected user.
3. Terra posts each normalized payload to your webhook. Other destinations include S3, SQL, MongoDB, Kafka and Supabase.
4. For history, you call the REST API with a date range.


plaintext


```text
GET https://api.tryterra.co/v2/activity?user_id=<terra_user_id>&start_date=2026-09-01&end_date=2026-09-30&to_webhook=true


dev-id: <your dev id>
x-api-key: <your api key>
```


Keep the range inside COROS's three-month window. Requests beyond it return nothing.


### The Activity payload


This is a sample COROS activity as Terra posts it to a webhook: a 25-minute strength session. The heart rate array is cut to three samples, and fields that are null or empty for this kind of session are left out.


```text
{
"type": "activity",
"version": "2022-03-16",
"status": "success",
"user": {
"user_id": "<terra_user_id>",
"reference_id": "<your_user_id>",
"created_at": "2026-11-25T11:37:01Z",
"provider": "COROS",
"last_webhook_update": null,
"scopes": "",
"active": true
},
"data": [
{
"metadata": {
"start_time": "2026-11-25T09:47:01.855000+00:00",
"end_time": "2026-11-25T10:12:01.855000+00:00",
"summary_id": "<activity_summary_id>",
"type": 80,
"upload_type": 1,
"name": "strength",
"timestamp_localization": 1
},
"device_data": {
"manufacturer": "COROS",
"name": "VERTIX 4"
},
"active_durations_data": {
"activity_seconds": 1500
},
"calories_data": {
"total_burned_calories": 244
},
"distance_data": {
"summary": { "distance_meters": 0 }
},
"heart_rate_data": {
"summary": {
"avg_hr_bpm": 100.5,
"max_hr_bpm": 112,
"min_hr_bpm": 63
},
"detailed": {
"hr_samples": [
{ "timestamp": "2026-11-25T09:47:01.855000+00:00", "bpm": 63, "context": 0, "timer_duration_seconds": 0 },
{ "timestamp": "2026-11-25T09:47:02.855000+00:00", "bpm": 65, "context": 0, "timer_duration_seconds": 1 },
{ "timestamp": "2026-11-25T09:47:03.855000+00:00", "bpm": 64, "context": 0, "timer_duration_seconds": 2 }
]
}
},
"data_enrichment": {
"efficiency_score": 99.4,
"strain_score": 100,
"rcrs_score": 100,
"trimp_score": 199.7
}
}
]
}
```


The full payload also carries these objects, all empty for a strength session:` lap_data` ,` position_data` ,` movement_data` ,` power_data` ,` MET_data` ,` TSS_data` ,` oxygen_data` ,` energy_data` ,` work_data` ,` polyline_map_data` and` strength_data` . A run or a ride fills the position, movement and distance objects. Field definitions are in Terra's[data models](https://docs.tryterra.co/reference/health-and-fitness-api/data-models) .


Six things to know when you parse it.


- **The envelope tells you what arrived.**` type` is the payload type and` version` is the schema version. The` user` block carries Terra's` user_id` , the` provider` , and` reference_id` , which is your own ID for that user.
- **Heart rate is per second.** Each sample has a timestamp, a` bpm` value, and` timer_duration_seconds` counting from the start of the activity. A 25-minute session carries 1,500 of them.
- ` **metadata.type**` **is a numeric enum.** 80 is strength training, 8 is running, 149 is trail running, 16 is road biking. Unrecognized types come back as 108.
- **Empty is not always null.** Summary values are` null` . Sample arrays and coordinates are` \[\]` .` strength_data` is` null` as a whole object. Check for both before you read.
- **Deduplicate on**` **metadata.summary_id**` **.** The same activity can arrive more than once with updated data. Update your stored record instead of adding a new one.
- **Terra does not alter provider readings.** It standardizes units and JSON shape and leaves the values as COROS reported them. Derived scores such as` trimp_score` and` strain_score` sit separately in` data_enrichment` . The same payload is also available as a FIT file or in FHIR format.


That is good news for anyone building on COROS, which is one of our favorite integrations to work with. Terra's analysis of[571 London Marathon runners](https://tryterra.co/research/london-marathon-data) found COROS heart rate and GPS data statistically indistinguishable from the most common watch in the field. Pair that with per-second samples, original FIT files and an API that keeps opening up, and COROS is a source we are glad to build on.


### The Daily and Sleep payloads


These are where COROS health data lands. The table maps what COROS exposes to the field it belongs to in Terra's schema.


COROS metric Payload Field in Terra's schema


Steps Daily` distance_data.steps`


Calories Daily` calories_data.total_burned_calories`


Resting heart rate Daily` heart_rate_data.summary.resting_hr_bpm`


Average heart rate Daily` heart_rate_data.summary.avg_hr_bpm`


Stress Daily` stress_data.avg_stress_level`


Sleep stages Sleep` sleep_durations_data.asleep.duration_deep_sleep_state_seconds` and the light and REM equivalents


Awake time Sleep` sleep_durations_data.awake.duration_awake_state_seconds`


Sleep timeline Sleep` sleep_durations_data.hypnogram_samples\[\]`


Overnight HRV Sleep` heart_rate_data.summary.avg_hrv_rmssd`


Naps Sleep` metadata.is_nap`


Daily payloads deduplicate differently from activities. The key is` metadata.start_time` and` metadata.end_time` together, and a Daily can arrive several times in one day as the step count grows.


### Writing back to COROS


The integration is not read-only. Terra's planned workouts[reached COROS in February 2026](https://tryterra.co/blog/february-2026-product-update) , so a structured workout built in your app can land on the user's watch.


## Live streaming: which COROS watches can send real-time data


No COROS cloud API streams data during a workout. Live data comes from one place only: the watch broadcasting heart rate over Bluetooth.


### The cloud path is near real time, not real time


Path When data arrives


Partner API webhook Within about 5 minutes of a workout


Build on COROS MCP When your app polls


COROS through Terra Up to 5 to 10 minutes after the watch syncs


All three depend on the watch syncing to the[COROS](https://tryterra.co/integrations/coros) app first. A workout recorded without the phone nearby arrives when the user next syncs.


### The live path is HR Broadcast


COROS watches can act as a heart rate monitor for other devices and apps. COROS calls this HR Broadcast, and its[pairing guide](https://tryterra.co/integrations/coros) describes it as a feature of COROS watches generally, over Bluetooth.


Device Live heart rate over Bluetooth Notes


PACE 3 Yes Named in COROS's Bluetooth device list


PACE 4 Yes Named in COROS's Bluetooth device list


PACE Pro Yes Named in COROS's Bluetooth device list


NOMAD Yes Named in COROS's Bluetooth device list


APEX 2 and 2 Pro Yes Named in COROS's Bluetooth device list


APEX 4 Yes Named in COROS's Bluetooth device list


VERTIX 2 and 2S Yes Named in COROS's Bluetooth device list


PACE 4 Pro Expected Too new to appear in the guide


VERTIX 4 Expected Too new to appear in the guide


HR Monitor armband Yes Up to 3 simultaneous Bluetooth connections


The signal is standard Bluetooth heart rate. Anything that reads a chest strap can read a COROS watch in broadcast mode. That includes[Terra's Streaming API](https://docs.tryterra.co/streaming-api/getting-started) , which delivers readings from Bluetooth and ANT+ devices to your backend roughly once per second.


### COROS VERTIX 4: what changed, and what it means for the data


The VERTIX 4 is COROS's new flagship expedition watch. It brings the hardware COROS has introduced across the PACE 4, PACE 4 Pro, NOMAD and APEX 4 over the past 18 months to the top of the range, and it is the first major VERTIX update since the VERTIX 2.


#### The latest heart rate sensor


The VERTIX 4 carries COROS's newest optical heart rate sensor, the same one found in its other recent watches. For developers, that means heart rate from a VERTIX 4 arrives in the same shape and at the same per-second resolution as the rest of the current lineup. Users who train with a chest strap or the COROS HR Monitor can pair it to the watch, and those readings land in the same heart rate object.


#### Three satellite modes


The watch offers GPS only, all systems and multi-band modes, with all systems as the default. Whichever mode a user picks, the track arrives in` position_data` as timestamped coordinates.


#### Nothing changes in your integration


A VERTIX 4 syncs through the same COROS account and the same endpoints as every other COROS device. Activities, daily summaries and sleep come through the same Terra payloads, so an app that already supports COROS supports the VERTIX 4 from day one.


## What the VERTIX 4 tells us about where COROS is heading


Read the launch next to the API changes and the direction is a good one for anyone building on COROS data.


- **One sensor platform across the range.** The VERTIX 4 uses the same heart rate sensor as other recent COROS watches. For developers, that means consistent data across a COROS user base, whichever watch a user wears.
- **COROS is opening its data up.** It has shipped five API updates since May, published its documentation, and added write access. COROS says athletes should own their data and choose where it goes, and its roadmap this year backs that up.
- **Training data is the strength.** Per-second heart rate, original FIT files, laps, running power and training load make COROS a rich source of workout data. Health coverage is growing too: June added time series for stress and overnight HRV.
- **Live heart rate is already possible.** HR Broadcast uses the standard Bluetooth heart rate profile, so a COROS watch can feed a real-time product today without extra hardware.
